text:
By the time I reached my mother’s house, the sun had softened the tar in the road. The paint on the Congregational church blistered in the heat, and a plastic flag hung limp outside the pharmacy. My mother, eighty-four and convinced a person could improve a day by getting up early enough, had been waiting on the porch since nine.

“You’re late,” she said.

It was eleven-thirty. She wore a straw hat with a brown ribbon and held a dish towel over one arm, as if I’d arrived to be put to work.

“I stopped for coffee.”

“You could have had coffee here.”

“I know.”

I kissed her cheek and followed her inside.

The house was small and square, with a kitchen my father had probably added and a porch he had built. The yellow floor tiles I remembered from childhood had faded to old butter, except beneath the refrigerator, where they were bright.

A bowl of apricots sat on the table, two bruised.

“You brought the good ones,” I said.

“I bought them at the farm stand.”

“I mean, you saved them.”

She gave me a look. “You can have one.”

My visits were arranged a week ahead, then confirmed by two more phone calls. On the day itself, she acted as if I’d appeared without warning. She asked if I was hungry, announced there was nothing in the house, and produced lunch.

While she put coffee on, I took my bag upstairs to the bedroom that had been mine before college and, later, for good. On the dresser sat a photograph of my brother and me at the beach, white with sun lotion. My mother’s arm entered the frame from the right. She’d taken the picture and missed getting herself in it. I’d once thought that was modesty. It may have been habit.

Downstairs, she’d set out toast and strawberry jam, dark and soft, with seeds that caught between your teeth. She remembered I liked it. She did not remember I’d stopped taking sugar in coffee.

“It’s too hot to eat,” she said, buttering her toast.

“It’s not too hot to eat.”

“You’re not the one who has to stand over the stove.”

“You haven’t stood over the stove.”

“I made coffee.”

“Coffee isn’t a stove.”

She glanced toward it, then laughed—a short, surprised sound.

We ate beneath the kitchen clock, stopped at 2:17. She’d been promising to get a new battery for six years. A bank calendar nearby was turned to May though it was June. In blue ink she’d written “Dentist,” “call L.,” “Tomatoes,” and “rain?” Some notes were crossed out; others had question marks.

After lunch, she insisted we see the garden.

“I thought it was too hot to stand over the stove,” I said.

“It’s not the same thing.”

Behind the garage were four raised beds. Tomatoes were tied to stakes with strips of cloth, beans climbed a trellis, and marigolds bordered the rows.

“You don’t have to do all this,” I said.

“I don’t do all of it. The plants do most of it.”

She bent to pull a weed. I noticed how carefully she moved, calculating each step. Her knees were stiff, and her left hand trembled as she reached for the trowel.

“Let me do that.”

“I know what’s a weed.”

“I wasn’t saying you didn’t.”

“People think they’re being helpful when they take things away from you.”

I accepted the rebuke and pulled weeds while she supervised. She told me the neighbor’s boy had begun mowing lawns, the library was closing early on Wednesdays, and a woman from church had broken her wrist and was “making a fuss about it.”

“You complain,” I said.

“I don’t make a fuss.”

“About what?”

“People making a fuss.”

At the far end of the garden stood my father’s old shed, built from salvaged boards. His initials were carved into one corner, though mildew had nearly swallowed them. My mother said she’d asked the town to take it away, but they never did.

“You could hire someone to take care of the yard,” I said.

“I take care of the yard.”

“I mean when you can’t.”

“When I can’t, I’ll know.”

I didn’t ask what she meant.

Inside, she made iced tea with lemon and no sugar. We sat in the living room with the curtains drawn. She asked about my work. I shortened the story, leaving out the trouble with the grant and my thoughts of moving. She asked whether my daughter was still “seeing that boy.” I said she was, though the boy had long since become a young man.

Then she asked if I remembered the time we drove to the ocean in a thunderstorm.

“I remember you stopping at every gas station to ask for directions.”

“I didn’t stop at every gas station.”

“You stopped at three.”

“You were a child. You don’t remember things accurately.”

We’d taken the wrong road and reached a beach beneath a nearly black sky. My brother cried because the waves were too loud. My mother carried him to the car while my father and I stood in the rain, laughing. In her telling, my father had been lost and I had been frightened. The past never stayed put. It moved toward whoever needed it.

“You always liked the water,” she said.

“I still do.”

“You used to go in until you were blue.”

“I was a kid.”

“You were stubborn.”

“You liked that about me.”

“I didn’t say I didn’t.”

Around four, she suggested we go to the hardware store.

“You need something?”

“Light bulbs.”

“I can get them.”

“You don’t know which ones.”

She found her purse. At the door, she checked the lock, then checked it again. It used to irritate me. Now I waited while she turned the key, tugged the knob, and turned it once more.

The store was three streets away. We drove with the windows open because the air-conditioning had stopped working. On Main Street, she pointed out where the bakery had been, the vacant lot where the movie theater stood, and the new dental office that used to be the house of a man who once chased me off his lawn.

“You were always in trouble with him,” she said.

“I was ten.”

“He didn’t like children.”

“He had a sign that said KEEP OFF THE GRASS.”

“Exactly.”

She bought four light bulbs, though she needed only two, and added screws and hand soap. The cashier asked how she was managing in the heat.

“Fine,” my mother said. “I’m not made of sugar.”

Outside, she paused in the bright parking lot, as if the town had shifted while we were inside. I offered to drive home. She said she knew the way.

Back on the porch, she took off her hat and set it on a chair. She fetched the dish towel, then asked if I wanted to stay for dinner. I said I couldn’t; I’d planned to leave before dark.

“You don’t have to go.”

“I have an early start tomorrow.”

“You always have an early start.”

I stood by the car, my bag in the passenger seat, trying to find a sentence that would make leaving feel less like leaving. She touched my sleeve.

“You’ll come again?”

“Of course.”

“When?”

“Soon.”

I kissed her cheek. Her skin was warm and dry. Driving out of town, I saw her in the mirror on the porch, still holding the towel. At the first stop sign, I looked back. The house had disappeared behind the trees.

A month later, my brother called to say she’d been taken to the hospital. She had gone out to the garden during the hottest part of the day and fallen beside the bean trellis. A neighbor found her. The doctors called it heatstroke; my brother called it sunstroke, as if the older word might make the event less clinical. For two days she didn’t know where she was. Then she knew, and wanted to go home.

She spent ten days in the hospital and another week at a rehabilitation place near the highway. By the time I arrived, she’d been home for three days. I had come as soon as I could, which sounds more decisive than it is.

The house looked unchanged from the road, except for a new handrail on the steps and the porch chair moved closer to the door. My mother sat in the living room with her legs under a blanket. Her hair lay in soft, flattened waves against her head. She had lost weight. The straw hat was on the hall table, its ribbon turned inside out.

“You came,” she said.

“I did.”

“They tell you I had a little spell.”

“They said you had sunstroke.”

“Same thing.”

I sat beside her. On the table was a glass of water and a card listing the signs of dehydration. She had folded it in half. My brother had left food in the refrigerator and a note in large letters: SOUP IS IN THE BLUE POT. She said she didn’t need anyone to tell her where the soup was, though the pot was in the sink.

“How are you feeling?”

“Fine.”

“Are you tired?”

“No.”

“Dizzy?”

“No.”

She lifted one hand to end the interview. It trembled more than before, but she seemed not to notice.

The kitchen clock still read 2:17. The calendar still showed May, though it was July. The yellow squares on the floor glowed beneath the refrigerator.

I asked if she remembered my last visit.

“Of course.”

“What did we do?”

“We had lunch.”

“We went to the hardware store.”

“Did we?”

“You bought light bulbs.”

“I might have.”

“We went out to the garden, too.”

She looked toward the window. “I was out there?”

“Yes. You showed me the tomatoes.”

“Did I get anything done?”

“You showed me the tomatoes.”

“That’s not getting anything done.”

She seemed displeased, as if I’d praised the wrong thing. I told her the tomatoes were doing well. She asked whether the beans had climbed the trellis. I said they had. She closed her eyes, not asleep, just resting them.

On the hall table, beside her hat, lay the dish towel from that day, folded into a precise square. A few dry leaves were caught in the hat’s ribbon.

In the kitchen, the light bulbs were still in their paper bag, along with the screws and hand soap. One apricot had collapsed on the tablecloth, leaving a dark spot. I wrapped it in a paper towel. The fruit bowl was empty except for a pit.

I thought of the things from that day: the coffee she made after saying there was nothing in the house; the weeds I pulled under her direction; her hand on the key as she checked the lock. They had seemed like habits, and they were habits, but they were also how she kept the world arranged to her liking. She had chosen which weeds I could pull. She had bought four bulbs instead of two. She had waited for me with a towel over her arm, taking care of what she could reach.

When I returned to the living room, she was awake.

“I was thinking,” she said, “we should go to the hardware store.”

“What for?”

“Light bulbs.”

“I saw them in the kitchen.”

“Oh.” She considered this. “Then we don’t need to go.”

“Not today.”

She nodded. We sat in the dim room, curtains drawn against the afternoon. The mower outside stopped. Somewhere in the house, a pipe clicked as it cooled.

After a while, my mother asked if I remembered the trip to the ocean.

“I do,” I said.

“You were frightened of the waves.”

“I might have been.”

“They were loud.”

“They were.”

She leaned back against the cushion. Her eyes stayed open, but her attention seemed to drift toward the window, where the light had begun to soften.

“I always liked the water,” she said.

“I know.”

It was something she’d said before, or perhaps something new. I couldn’t tell whether she was remembering the beach or telling me about herself. I didn’t correct her. I sat beside her until the room grew dark enough that the mantel clock was difficult to read. It was seven minutes fast, as always. Outside, the town cooled by degrees. Inside, her hand rested open on the blanket, as if waiting for someone to place something there.
